title: 006 — Python 3.15: lazy imports, frozendict, UTF-8 by default and a faster JIT

006 — Python 3.15: lazy imports, frozendict, UTF-8 by default and a faster JIT

The one idea: Python 3.15 is the new stable Python. The changes that matter most for data and backend work are lazy import for faster startup, a built-in frozendict, UTF-8 as the default text encoding everywhere (Windows included), and a JIT that is now measurably faster. Check the UTF-8 change before you upgrade: it can change how existing scripts read files.

Added 2026-10-10 · Released 2026-10-09 by the Python core team

1. What it is

Python 3.15.0 is the annual feature release. The headline changes:

Area Change PEP
Startup Explicit lazy import 810
Built-ins frozendict, an immutable, hashable dict 814
Built-ins sentinel type for unique marker values 661
Syntax Unpacking (* and **) inside comprehensions 798
I/O UTF-8 is the default encoding, whatever the OS locale 686
Performance JIT upgrade: about 7–8% faster on x86-64 Linux, 11–12% on Apple Silicon macOS (vs the tail-calling interpreter) —
Tooling New profiling package with Tachyon, a sampling profiler 799
Typing TypedDict extra items, TypeForm, disjoint bases 728, 747, 800
Build Frame pointers on by default, which helps profilers 831

The official macOS installers now include free-threading support by default.

2. Why it matters

  • Faster CLIs, jobs and serverless functions. Big imports (pandas, cloud SDKs) slow down every start. lazy import defers the cost until the module is first used, which helps short-lived scripts, Azure Functions and Databricks job entry points.
  • Fewer encoding bugs. Code that ran on Linux and then broke on Windows with UnicodeDecodeError was nearly always about the default encoding. With UTF-8 as the default, files read the same way on every OS.
  • Safer shared config. frozendict gives you an immutable mapping you can use as a dict key, cache key or module-level constant without a third-party package.
  • Free speed. The JIT gains need no code change.

3. How it works

---
title: lazy import — when the cost is paid
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Script start
    participant L as lazy import json
    participant U as First use of json
    S->>L: name bound, module not loaded
    Note over S: startup continues quickly
    S->>U: json.loads(...)
    U->>U: module loads now

A lazy import binds the name at once, but the module is only loaded on first use. It is allowed only at module level. Inside a function, a class body or try/except/finally, it raises SyntaxError.

4. How to use it

Install 3.15 next to your current version, for example with uv python install 3.15 or the python.org installer, and run your tests on it.

Lazy imports (from the "What's New" docs):

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

print("Starting up...")  # json and pathlib are not fully imported yet

data = json.loads('{"key": "value"}')  # json gets fully imported here
p = Path(".")  # pathlib gets fully imported here

frozendict:

>>> a = frozendict(x=1, y=2)
>>> a['z'] = 3
TypeError: 'frozendict' object does not support item assignment
>>> hash(a) == hash(frozendict(y=2, x=1))
True

Unpacking in comprehensions:

>>> lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
>>> [*L for L in lists]          # flatten
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
>>> {**d for d in dicts}         # merge, later keys win
{'a': 3, 'b': 2}

UTF-8 default: open('data.csv') now reads UTF-8 on every OS. To get the old locale-based behaviour back, set PYTHONUTF8=0 or run with -X utf8=0. The safest habit is still to pass encoding= explicitly.

In practice, an upgrade checklist:

  1. Search for open( calls with no encoding= that read files from Windows systems with a legacy code page. These may now decode differently.
  2. Read the "Removed" section of the What's New page. Modules such as pathlib, typing, datetime, http.server and importlib.resources lost deprecated APIs.
  3. Check that your key packages (pandas, PySpark, numpy, Azure SDKs) publish 3.15 wheels before moving production.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • Library support lags. Compiled packages need new wheels. Databricks runtimes and Azure Functions adopt new Python versions some time after release.
  • Lazy imports change when errors appear. A missing module fails at first use, not at startup. Keep normal imports for dependencies that must fail fast.
  • UTF-8 default can break legacy files. CSVs exported from older Windows tools in cp1252 will need an explicit encoding="cp1252".
  • macOS 27.0 note: the release post warns that IDLE and other tkinter apps may hang when opening dialogs from menus on macOS 27.0.
  • Adopt now or wait? Use 3.15 now for new tools and local scripts. Move production pipelines once your runtime (Databricks, Functions) and key packages support it.

6. Where it fits

  • Python and data engineering: the language features data pipelines rely on.
  • Polars deep dive: a library to check for 3.15 wheels before upgrading.
  • Observability and performance: profiling, where the new sampling profiler and frame pointers help.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why can lazy import hide a missing dependency until much later in a run?
  2. A script reads a CSV fine on Linux but fails on a Windows build agent. Which 3.15 change fixes that, and what is the safer habit anyway?
  3. When would you choose frozendict over a plain dict or a MappingProxyType?
  4. Rewrite [x for L in lists for x in L] with 3.15 syntax.
  5. What do you check before moving a Databricks job to 3.15?

Sources

  • What's new in Python 3.15 — Python docs
